paragraphs.text: He is good, and doeth good, Psa 119:68, not to his Israel only, as is set forth in the two foregoing psalms, but to all mankind, which is Divini ingenii cura, as one saith, whatever atheists and epicures say to the contrary, denying a Divine providence: witness that profane distich of theirs:
paragraphs.anchor: O give thanks unto the Lord, for he is good

paragraphs.text: Nempe nihil positum est, et sors incerta vagatur,
Fertque refertque vices, et habent mortalia casum.
For his mercy endureth for ever] Notwithstanding men’s many and mighty provocations.
Four sorts of whom are afterwards instanced: 1. exiles; 2. prisoners; 3. sick persons; 4. seamen. These and the like must praise him in a special manner for their deliverance.
paragraphs.anchor: Let the redeemed of the Lord

paragraphs.text: Or, of distress.
paragraphs.anchor: From the hand of the enemy

paragraphs.text: He beginneth with wayfaring men and exiles, because, according to Tyrtaeus, Non exul curae dicitur esse Deo.
paragraphs.anchor: And gathered them out of the lands

paragraphs.text: Heb. from the sea, that is, as the Chaldee expoundeth it, from the southern sea, called the Red Sea.
paragraphs.anchor: And from the south

paragraphs.text: This is a sad case, Mendicum patria amissa laribusque vagari.
paragraphs.anchor: They wandered in the wilderness, &c.

paragraphs.text: Pλαγχθοσυνης ουκ εστι κακωτερον αλλο βροτοισι.
And yet this is the case of all God’s redeemed ones while they are here, Heb 11:38 1Pe 2:12.
Per varios casus per tot discrlmina rerum
Tendimus in patriam veram vitamque perennem.

The Lord’s exiles meet many times with the like exigents in the wilderness of this wicked world; but let them be content, and say, We are well for the present, and it will be better with us hereafter (Melancthon).
paragraphs.anchor: Hungry and thirsty, &c.

paragraphs.text: Exul erat Christus; comites nos exulis huius
Esse decet, cuius nos quoque membra sumus.

Though under a wrong name, it may be, as of Jupiter, Mercury, &c.; and, in an uncertain way, as Hecuba did with her, O Iupiter quicquid es sive caelum hoc, sive mens, quae vehitur in coelo, &c.; and as those mariners in Jon 1:5, who cried every man to his god, and, lest they might all mistake the true God, they awaken Jonah, to call upon his God.
paragraphs.anchor: Then they cried unto the Lord

paragraphs.text: Out of his general goodness and compassion to the poor creature; like as he heareth the young ravens that cry unto him, no otherwise than by implication only, and out of mere necessity. God is the Saviour of all men, but especially of those that believe.
paragraphs.anchor: And he delivered them out of their distresses

paragraphs.text: Better than that Dea Vibilia among the Romans, of whom they fancied that she set them right when out of the way at any time; or Minerva among the Athenians, who, they said, turned all their evil counsels to the best unto them.
paragraphs.anchor: And he led them forth by the right way

paragraphs.text: Grow to a state of settlement, to Jerusalem, saith the Chaldee; to that city which hath a foundation, may we say, whose maker and founder is God, Heb 11:10.
paragraphs.anchor: That they might go to a city of habitation

paragraphs.text: Heb. that they would confess it to the Lord, both in secret and in society. This is all the rent that God requireth; he is content that we have the comfort of his blessings, so he may have the honour of them. This was all the fee Christ looked for for his cures, Go and tell what God hath done for thee. Words seem to be a poor and slight recompense; but Christ, saith Nazianzen, calleth himself the Word.
paragraphs.anchor: Oh that men would praise the Lord, &c.

paragraphs.text: This as a recapitulation of the first part, Psa 107:5-7, and setteth forth the reason why the redeemed should praise God out of the sweet experience they have had of his wonderful providence and goodness toward them.
paragraphs.anchor: For he satisfieth the longing soul, &c.

paragraphs.text: This flower the blessed Virgin picketh out of David’s garden (among many others out of other parts of Holy Scripture, wherein it appeareth she was singularly well versed), and puts it into her posy, Luk 1:53.
paragraphs.anchor: And filleth the hungry soul with goodness

paragraphs.text: Here come in the second sort of God’s redeemed or rescued ones, viz. captives and prisoners, whose dark and doleful condition is in this verse described.
paragraphs.anchor: Such as sit in darkness, &c.

paragraphs.text: In dark caves and horrid prisons, where there is Luctus ubique payor, et plurima morris imago. Such was Joseph’s first prison, Jeremiah’s miry dungeon, Lollards’ tower, the bishop of London’s coalhouse, &c.
paragraphs.anchor: And in the shadow of death

paragraphs.text: Or, in poverty and iron, as Manasseh was. Many are the miseries that poor prisoners undergo. Good Savonarola had the experience of it, and Zegedine, and the martyrs, and various of God’s dear servants in the recent wars here. A certain pious prince, discoursing about the dangers that were to be then expected for the profession of religion, said, Nihil so magis metuere quam diuturnos carceres, that he feared nothing so much as perpetual imprisonment.
paragraphs.anchor: Being bound in affliction and iron

paragraphs.text: Sin is at the bottom of all men’s miseries, as the procreant cause thereof; for God afflicteth not willingly, nor grieveth the children of men, Lam 3:33, but they rebel against his words written in the Scriptures, or, at least, in their hearts; and so he is concerned in point of honour to subdue them.
paragraphs.anchor: Because they rebelled against the words of God

paragraphs.text: A foul fault. See Luk 7:30.
paragraphs.anchor: And contemned the counsel

paragraphs.text: That proud piece of flesh, Quod erat elatum et verba Dei contempsit, saith Kimchi, which had stouted it out with God, and thought to have carried it away with a strong hand; as Manasseh, that sturdy rebel, till God had hampered him, and laid him in cold irons.
paragraphs.anchor: Therefore he brought down their heart

paragraphs.text: See Psa 107:6.
paragraphs.anchor: Then they cried unto the Lord

paragraphs.text: This is comfort to the greatest sinners; if they can but find a praying heart, God will find a pitying heart, and rebels shall be received with all sweetness, if at length they return, though brought in by the cross.
paragraphs.anchor: And he saved them, &c.

paragraphs.text: He sent his mandamus {a}, as Psa 44:4, and that did the deed, as Act 5:19; Act 12:7.
paragraphs.anchor: He brought them out of darkness

paragraphs.text: {a} Originally applied generically to a number of ancient writs, letters missive, or mandates, issued by the sovereign, directing the performance of certain acts.
See Psa 107:8.
paragraphs.anchor: Oh that men, &c.

paragraphs.text: If Samson could do so, how much more the Almighty, whom nothing can withstand! Nature may be stopped in her course, as when the fire burned not. Men may not be able to do as they would. Angels, good or bad, may be hindered, because in them there is an essence and an executive power, between which God can step at his pleasure, and interpose his veto; but who or what shall hinder the Most High?
paragraphs.anchor: For he hath broken the gates of brass

paragraphs.text: Propter viam defectionis sum, by means of their defection, their departing away from the living God, through an evil heart of unbelief, Heb 3:12.
paragraphs.anchor: Fools because of their transgression

paragraphs.text: The flood gates whereof are set open, as it were, by that their defection from God; for now what should hinder?
paragraphs.anchor: And because of their iniquities

paragraphs.text: Heb. do afflict themselves, procure their own ruth, if not ruin, and so prove sinners against their own souls, as those, Num 16:30-33
paragraphs.anchor: Are afflicted

paragraphs.text: That is, their stomach loatheth it as unsavoury, though it be never so dainty: an appetite to our meat is an inconconceivable mercy, and, as we say, a sign of health.
paragraphs.anchor: Their soul abhorreth

paragraphs.text: Iam ipsum mortis limen pulsant; as till then little sense of sin or fear of the wrath to come. See Job 30:19-23. {See Trapp on "Job 30:19"} {See Trapp on "Job 30:20"} {See Trapp on "Job 30:21"} {See Trapp on "Job 30:22"} {See Trapp on "Job 30:23"}
paragraphs.anchor: And they draw near unto the gates of death

paragraphs.text: Quando medicus et medicinae non prosunt, saith Kimchi, when physicians have done their utmost. See Psa 107:6.
paragraphs.anchor: Then they cry, &c.

paragraphs.text: He commanded deliverance, and it was done; unless there he an allusion to the essential Word, who was afterwards to take flesh, and to heal the diseased.
paragraphs.anchor: He sent his word, and healed them

paragraphs.text: Heb. from their corrupting pits or graves, which do now even gape for them. And he calleth them theirs, quia per peccatum foderunt eas, saith Kimchi, because by their sin themselves have digged them.
paragraphs.anchor: And delivered them from their destructions

paragraphs.text: See Psa 107:8.
paragraphs.anchor: Oh that men, &c.

paragraphs.text: Men are misericordiis et miraculis obsesse, and it were no hard matter to find a miracle in most of our mercies.
paragraphs.anchor: And for his wonderful works

paragraphs.text: If they have escaped sickness, let them offer a passover; and if they have recovered, a thankoffering. Heathens in this case praised their Esculapius; Papists their Sebastian, Valentine, Apollonia, &c. Ears of wax they offer to the saint, who, as they suppose, cureth the ears; eyes of wax to the saint that cureth the eyes, &c. But it is Jehovah only who healeth us.
paragraphs.anchor: And let them sacrifice, &c.

paragraphs.text: Memorize and magnify them.
paragraphs.anchor: And declare his works, &c.

paragraphs.text: Here we have a fourth specimen or instance of God’s gracious and wise dispensations towards men, in their trading or trafficking by sea. These are said to go down to sea, because the banks are above it; but the water is naturally higher than the land, and, therefore, sailors observe that their ships fly faster to the shore than from it. But what a bold man, saith the poet, was he that first put forth to sea! (Horat. Od. lib. 1, 3.)
paragraphs.anchor: They that go down to the sea in ships

paragraphs.text: Illi robut, et aes triplex
Circa pectus erat, qui fragilem truci
Commisit pelago ratem
Primus, nec timuit praecipitem Africum, &c.
That do business in great waters] Merchants and mariners, who fish, and find almug, or coral, saith Kimchi, who do export and import commodities of all sorts.

In sea monsters, as whales and whirlpools, and sudden change of weather, and the like, not a few; ebbs and flows, pearls, islands, &c. These are just wonders, and may fully convince the most stubborn atheist that is.
paragraphs.anchor: These see the works of the Lord, &c.

paragraphs.text: Of this Seneca, though a heathen, could say, Inter caetera providentiae divinae opera hoc quoque dignum est admiratione, &c., Among other works of the Divine providence this is admirable, that the winds lie upon the sea for the furtherance of navigation, &c.
paragraphs.anchor: For he commandeth, and raiseth the stormy wind, &c.

paragraphs.text: An elegant hypotyposis or description of a storm at sea; like whereunto is that in Virgil,
paragraphs.anchor: They mount up to the heaven, they go down, &c.

paragraphs.text: Tollimur in coelum curvato gurgite, et iidem
Subducta ad manes imos descendimus unda.

Their soul is melted because of trouble] They are ready to die through fear of death. Juntas understandeth it of extreme vomiting, as if they were casting up their very hearts. Anacharsis for this cause doubted whether he should reckon mariners among the living or the dead. And another said, that any man will go to sea at first I wonder not; but to go a second time thither is little better than madness.
Natant nautae, et vacillant cerebro et pedibus.
paragraphs.anchor: They reel to and fro, &c.

paragraphs.text: And are at their wit’s end] All their skill and strength faileth them at once; they can do no more for their lives. Heb. All their wisdom is swallowed up; that is, the art of navigation is now to no use with them.
"Then," if ever: hence that speech of one, Qui nescit orare, discat navigare, He who cannot pray, let him go to sea, and there he will learn. See Psa 107:6.
paragraphs.anchor: Then they cry unto the Lord

paragraphs.text: "He," that is, God Almighty, whose the sea is, and he made it, Psa 95:5; not the Pagans Neptune, or the papagans’ St Nicholas.
paragraphs.anchor: He maketh the storm a calm

paragraphs.text: If, therefore, the voluptuous humours in our body (which is but as a cup made of the husk of an acorn in respect to the sea) will not be pacified when the Lord saith unto us, "Be still"; every drop of water in the sea will be a witness of our monstrous rebellion and disobedience.
paragraphs.anchor: So that the waves thereof are still

paragraphs.text: All is hushed on the sudden, as Mat 8:26, both their fears and the sea’s outrages being quickly reduced to a peaceable period.
paragraphs.anchor: Then are they glad because they be quiet

paragraphs.text: This is more than they then wished for: God is many times better to men than their prayers.
paragraphs.anchor: So he bringeth them to their desired haven

paragraphs.text: See Psa 107:8.
paragraphs.anchor: Oh that men would, &c.

paragraphs.text: i.e. In all public meetings, ecclesiastical and civil.
paragraphs.anchor: Let them exalt him also in the congregation, &c.

paragraphs.text: Hitherto the psalmist hath set forth God’s good providence in delivering men from several deaths and dangers; now he declareth the same in his just and powerful transmutations in nature, while according to the good pleasure of his will he changeth men’s condition, either from good to evil, or from evil to good, beyond all expectation; it is even he that doeth it, whatsoever a company of dizzy headed men dream to the contrary, as one phraseth it. It is God who drieth up those rivers, whereby the land was made fat and fertile, Isa 41:17.
paragraphs.anchor: He turneth rivers into a wilderness

paragraphs.text: Heb. saltness. See Luk 14:34-35 Deu 29:23 Jdg 9:45. Salt breedeth barrenness, by eating up the fat and moisture of the earth. Some think the psalmist here alludeth to Sodom and her sisters turned into the Red Sea.
paragraphs.anchor: A fruitful land into barrenness

paragraphs.text: Hereof Judea is at this day a noble instance (besides many parts of Asia and Africa, once very fruitful, now, since they became Mahometan, dry and desert). Judea, saith one, hath now only some few parcels of rich ground found in it; that men may guess the goodness of the cloth by the fineness of the shreds. Greece, which was once Sol et sal gentium, saith another, terrarum flos, fens literarum, nunc vel Priamo miseranda manus; - nunc in Graecia desideramus Graeciam; it is nothing like the place it was once.
paragraphs.anchor: For the wickedness of them that dwell therein

paragraphs.text: Some places, again, God (to show his power and providence) of sterile maketh to become fertile; Polonia, for instance, and other northern countries. Germany and France were of old full of woods and lakes, as Caesar and Tacitus testify; now it is otherwise. So in America to this day. So various desert places of Egypt and Ethiopia, when once they became Christians, became fruitful.
paragraphs.anchor: He turneth the wilderness, &c.

paragraphs.text: As our English, and other plantations in America, where sundry poor people get fair estates.
paragraphs.anchor: And there he maketh the hungry to dwell

paragraphs.text: The building of cities is of God, and so is their conservation.
paragraphs.anchor: That they may prepare a city

paragraphs.text: These are noble employments, such as the ancient patriarchs were much in, and the most honourable among the Romans, as Coriolanus, Marcus Curius, Cato Major, &c. Our forefathers, if they could call any one bonum eolonum, a good husbandman, they thought it praise enough, saith Cicero.
paragraphs.anchor: And sow the fields, and plant vineyards

paragraphs.text: The thankful earth yielding, by God’s blessing, her gratum onus, full burden to the laborious tiller.
paragraphs.anchor: Which may yield

paragraphs.text: See Pro 10:12 Psa 127:1 Jas 4:15. They are out that rest in natural causes.
paragraphs.anchor: He blesseth them also, &c.

paragraphs.text: Minorati sunt. This also is of the Lord, who hath treasuries of plagues, and cannot be exhausted.
paragraphs.anchor: Again, they are minished

paragraphs.text: See Job 12:21; Job 12:24, {See Trapp on "Job 12:21"} {See Trapp on "Job 12:24"} Poena tyrannorum est contemptus, exilium, nex, saith Genebrard. All the policy or king craft cannot save them.
paragraphs.anchor: He poureth contempt, &c.

paragraphs.text: The godly poor, as he did David.
paragraphs.anchor: Yet setteth he the poor

paragraphs.text: Of sheep, which multiply exceedingly in a short time.
paragraphs.anchor: And maketh him families like a flock

paragraphs.text: It shall cheer them up to see that the reins of government are in God’s hand; and to behold such love in such providence.
paragraphs.anchor: The righteous shall see it, and rejoice

paragraphs.text: Shall be down in the mouth, as we use to say, {see Job 5:16} and have her tongue chambered.
paragraphs.anchor: And all iniquity shall stop her mouth

paragraphs.text: Heb. Who is wise? q.d. not many. Exclamatio querulatoria (Piscat.). Rari quippe boni. None but those that observe providences, and lay up experiences; which, if men would do, they might have a divinity of their own, were they but well read in the story of their own lives.
paragraphs.anchor: Whoso is wise

paragraphs.text: And as for those providences that for present he understandeth not, reiecit in Dei abyssos; he believeth that there is a reason for them, and that they shall one day be unriddled.
paragraphs.anchor: Even they shall understand, &c.
